items.author: langchain
items.how: Each agent session is traced (a trace is the full record of what the agent did: messages, tool calls, tokens used). LangSmith now links each thread (a conversation with the agent) to the pull request it produced (a PR is a proposed code change that gets reviewed and merged). You see what a merged PR cost, and how much token spend never led to a PR. It works across harnesses (the software wrapper around the model) and model providers.
items.title: LangSmith Coding agent ROI: what each agent-written PR costs
items.try: A LangSmith feature (paid product with a limited free tier). The announcement link could not be read (t.co blocked), details limited to the tweet.
items.what: A new dashboard in LangSmith (LangChain's monitoring tool) that gathers every coding agent a team uses (Claude Code, Codex, etc.) and computes their return on investment. Put simply, an expense report per pull request.
items.who: Companies whose token bill is exploding. According to the team: see what each merged PR costs, who is shipping slop (sloppy code), and who deserves more tokens. The question any portfolio company will ask: do our agents earn more than they cost?

items.author: bentlegen
items.how: Version 1 was an autonomous AI PM agent. The founder's finding: nobody wants another agent, they want to use their own. So Modem was rebuilt as a platform: it collects and structures the problems, and the agents you already use (Claude, Codex...) pull from it. Technical details are not in the tweet.
items.title: Modem 2.0: an AI PM that works with your agents
items.try: Commercial product. Site not reachable (modem.dev), details limited.
items.what: A tool that digs through customer channels to find buried problems, tracks them, and follows up when the fix ships. Put simply, a product manager who reads all the customer feedback for you.
items.who: Product and ops teams drowning in customer feedback. Business lesson: it is better to be the data source agents consult than yet another agent.

items.author: nathanflurry
items.how: 1) First version: one prompt asking for the ticket severity with definitions of each level. Results were meh, because jev does not reason, by design. 2) Working version: split into tiny yes/no questions (did their service go down? are they blocked with no workaround? is something in Rivet broken?) and plain if-logic in code decides the severity. 3) Improvement loop: every misclassified ticket is given to an LLM with the expected result; the LLM adds it to a test suite, adjusts the decision logic, then backtests it on old tickets. Within a few tickets the classifier was solid. Counts: 13 questions for support classification and customer status, 6 for severity, 6 for follow-up timing.
items.title: Rivet's support ticket classifier: 13 tiny questions, not one big prompt
items.try: An experience report, not a product. jev is not documented in the tweet (no link).
items.what: How Rivet built the internal tool that triages its support tickets (severity, customer status, follow-up timing...) with a decision tool called jev.
items.who: Any ops or support automation. The most reusable pattern of the day: the model answers simple questions, code makes the decision, so it is controllable, monitorable and testable.

items.author: sydneyrunkle
items.how: Per the README: sub-agents (delegate a subtask to an agent with its own context window, its separate working memory), a filesystem (read, write, search), context management (summarize long threads, offload large tool outputs to disk), shell access in a sandbox (an isolated environment), persistent memory across sessions, human-in-the-loop (approve or reject an action before it runs), skills and MCP tools. Built on LangGraph. New yesterday: day-0 support for Gemini 4 Neon in Managed Deep Agents.

items.who: Building agents that handle long tasks in a company (research, ops) without reinventing the plumbing.
